instruments.name: Hohenpeißenberg Observatory
instruments.description: A mountain observatory site. Hohenpeißenberg in Bavaria holds one of the longest unbroken weather records in the world, with observations running since 1781 - which makes its measurement series a reference for studying long-term climate change.

instruments.name: Storm Warning Station Lindau
instruments.description: A lakeside storm-warning beacon. Around German lakes the flash rate is the message: 40 flashes per minute is a strong-wind warning, 90 flashes per minute is a storm warning - readable from a boat long before the weather arrives.

instruments.name: Automatic Measuring Station
instruments.description: An unstaffed automatic station. Sensors sit at standardised heights on the masts so that readings are comparable between sites, and the station reports on its own at fixed intervals, day and night, with no observer present.

instruments.name: Marine Measuring Platform
instruments.description: A marine/coastal measurement platform. Instruments over water face salt spray and constant motion, so the hardware is built to survive the environment it is measuring.

instruments.name: Measurement Field
instruments.description: An open measurement field carrying an array of sensors. Keeping the surroundings clear matters as much as the instruments: obstacles, buildings and trees would distort wind and radiation readings.

instruments.name: Airport Weather Station
instruments.description: Aviation weather instrumentation. Anemometers sit near the runway thresholds and a ceilometer measures cloud base, because for aviation the decisive numbers are crosswind, visibility and cloud height.

instruments.name: Radar Site
instruments.description: A radar installation. Radar does not sample a single point - it scans the surrounding volume of atmosphere, which is what makes area-wide precipitation maps and nowcasting possible.

instruments.name: Norderney Island Station
instruments.description: A North Sea island station. Coastal and island sites cover the sea-to-land transition, where the temperature contrast between water and land drives local wind and fog.
